title: P-split formulations: a class of intermediate formulations between big-M and convex hull for disjunctive constraints
contribution: A family of MIP formulations for disjunctive constraints (read as arXiv v3). Each additively separable constraint is split into P parts and the extended hull of the linearised disjunction is taken. The family equals big-M at P=1, is monotone in P under additive bounds, gives the convex hull at P=n for linear disjuncts and never gives it for fully disjoint strictly convex ones; on 344 instances intermediate P beats both extremes.
problem_entry: Big-M is light but weak and the extended convex hull is sharp but heavy, and folklore says hull formulations underperform; the paper aims at compact approximations of the hull for disjunctions with many variables and few constraints per disjunct (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Lift each constraint into P partial sums with variables alpha, make the x-constraints global so the disjunction becomes linear in alpha, then take the extended convex hull in the small alpha space; the auxiliary-variable count is independent of n (pp. 4-5, Remark 2).
assumptions: Convex additively separable g, bounded over X, minimal alpha variables, |C_l| << n (Assumptions 1-4, p. 3; sufficient, not necessary); a strict hierarchy needs additive bounds (Def. 3, p. 7); only globally valid bounds are used (p. 4); box domain for the nonconvex extension (p. 14).
proof_devices: Fourier-Motzkin elimination of auxiliary and disaggregated variables shows 1-split = big-M with the smallest valid M (Thm 1, pp. 6-7; Thm 4, p. 11)
Hierarchy by constraint aggregation: relaxing the (P+1)-split by summing two split blocks recovers the P-split under additive bounds (Thm 2, pp. 7-8; Cor. 1 strictness, p. 8)
Non-extended realisation for two-term disjunctions by repeated FM elimination, doubling the constraints at each step (Thm 3, pp. 9-10)
Invertible linear map alpha = Gamma x gives the convex hull for affine disjuncts at P = n (Thm 5, pp. 11-12; Cor. 3, p. 12)
Impossibility (ceiling) theorem via the midpoint of two extreme points on a hull facet and Jensen's inequality, for fully disjoint strictly convex disjunctions (Thm 6, pp. 12-13)
Redundancy criterion for linking constraints by bound additivity (Prop. 2, p. 13)
Separability of convex envelopes over a box (Horst-Tuy, Prop. 4, p. 15) lifts the results to nonconvex disjuncts (Cor. 4-5, p. 16)
experiments: 344 instances (clustering, P_ball, optimal sparse input features of ReLU NNs, semi-supervised clustering) in Gurobi 9 with a 1800 s limit, MIPFocus=3 and Cuts=1, and PreMIQCPForm=2 given to the hull only. Reported: average time/nodes, or remaining gap. Intermediate P is best, the best P varies by class, OBBT time is excluded, and two machines were used (pp. 18-26).
positioning: Balas-Grossmann disjunctive-programming lineage. Explicitly not an exact-hull paper ('The motivation behind the P-split formulations is different'). Links to factorable programming (ANTIGONE/SCIP), RLT and Belotti 2013; extends the authors' CPAIOR 2021 and NeurIPS 2021 papers (pp. 2-4, 13, 16).
writing: 'Best of both' framing; illustrative figures before theorems, including one where the hierarchy fails without additive bounds; plain admissions ('no advantage', 'merely of theoretical interest'); hedged 'promising potential'; small slips (Corallary, disjoint for disjunct, Table 4 caption) (pp. 1-2, 6-8, 12, 25-26).
limits_future: No rule for choosing P (the optimal P varies by class); needs the Assumptions 1-4 structure and is inadvisable otherwise; cut selection, linking-constraint selection and practical local bounds are left open (pp. 10, 14, 17, 22, 26).

method_links.note: Full text of the family the method cites: endpoints proven (Thm 1, Thm 5), hierarchy proven (Thm 2, Cor. 3), order-of-magnitude claim confirmed, family shipped as a Pyomo.GDP plugin and an OMLT partitioning strategy

No random-partition or deliberately weak control in this paper: partitioning by ordered index, with 'little variation' from other strategies stated but not tabulated; the best P varies by class, and only a range of 2-4 variables per split is recommended
Baseline strengthened (PreMIQCPForm=2 only for the hull); local bounds excluded to avoid an unfair advantage
Single solver, two different machines, OBBT bound time excluded from Table 4 (the same lapse SKILL.md notes for NeurIPS 2021)

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: ceiling theorem for one's own family
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Proves that no P-split can form the convex hull of a fully disjoint, strictly convex disjunction, alongside the hierarchy and linear-case attainment results

transferable: Prove the bottom endpoint of a formulation family by Fourier-Motzkin projection onto the original variables (pp. 6-7)
Prove monotonicity by showing that the coarser member is the finer one with constraint blocks aggregated (pp. 7-8)
State and prove where the family cannot reach the ideal formulation (pp. 12-13)
Discard redundant pairwise linking constraints with a bound-additivity test before adding them (p. 13)
Give the heavy baseline its own best solver flag and document the asymmetry; exclude strengthenings that only your method can use (pp. 17, 21-22)
Report the average remaining gap instead of time when more than half of a class times out (p. 24)

quotes.text: Our numerical comparisons do not include locally valid bounds on the α-variables, as such bounds are typically not easily obtainable and could give the P-split formulations an unfair advantage.
Without this structure, the P-split formulations do not necessarily have an advantage over either the big-M or convex hull formulation.

title: Beyond adjacency: Graph encoding with reachability and shortest paths
contribution: A general integer-programming encoding of graph spaces with reachability, shortest distances and on-path indicators, proved exact by a bijection theorem. Subclasses (undirected, connected, DAG, st-DAG, weakly connected) are obtained by adding linear constraints, the encoding shrinks to O(n^2) under strong connectivity, and lexicographic symmetry-breaking constraints are proved to keep every isomorphism class.
problem_entry: Graph optimisation relies on heuristics or latent-space generative models that learn feasibility, lack optimality and are problem-specific; adjacency variables alone carry no connectivity, reachability or distance information (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Introduce r, d and delta variables tied to adjacency A through eight necessary conditions linearised with explicit big-Ms; specialise by adding constraints; keep only single-source distances under strong connectivity; break symmetry by the lexicographic order of neighbour or successor sets (pp. 2-15).
assumptions: Labelled nodes for the encoding; node count in [n0, n] with existing nodes indexed first; symmetry analysis on (weakly) connected n-node graphs; explicit big-M coefficients; power-of-two coefficients acknowledged as numerically unstable for large n (pp. 2-4, 10, 16).
proof_devices: Necessity (Lemma 1), then sufficiency: bijection proved by induction on min(d_uv(G), d_uv), with two cases and contradiction sub-cases (Thm 1, pp. 4-6)
The same induction for the single-source O(n^2) encoding (Thm 2, pp. 8-9)
Strong connectivity as the intersection of the encoding on G and on its transpose (Lemma 2, p. 9)
Constructive completeness of symmetry breaking: indexing Algorithm 1 with temporary indices, Props 1-3 and Lemma 3, contradiction at the minimal violating index (Thm 3, pp. 11-13)
The lexicographic neighbour constraint implies the older connectivity-ordering constraint (Lemma 4, pp. 13-14)
Reverse-topological Algorithm 2 for the DAG successor-set constraints (Thm 4, Props 5-6, pp. 14-15)
Conjecture 1 stated openly and verified numerically only for n <= 7 (pp. 15-16)
experiments: No timing study. Feasible solutions are counted with Gurobi PoolSearchMode=2 (cap 10^6) and bracketed by the OEIS labelled and unlabelled counts, e.g. connected undirected n=7: 1,866,256 -> 3,628 vs 853 (Table 4, p. 16); worked example 720 -> 4 indexings (p. 11).
positioning: Distils the group's application papers [45-48] into a general setting. Joins constraint-based symmetry handling (Margot, Liberti, Hojny, Kaibel-Pfetsch orbitopes) and generalises orbitope lexicographic ordering from bipartite graphs to arbitrary undirected graphs; extends McDonald et al. (pp. 2, 10, 16).
writing: 'Necessary conditions, then sufficiency' announced up front; each condition given in words, in logic, then in linear form with a named big-M; catalogue table with OEIS ids; worked appendix examples; low hedging; several copy-editing slips (pp. 1-4, 10, 14).
limits_future: Numerical instability of the 2^(n-u-1) coefficients, an unproven conjecture, small-scale experiments only; future work: more graph properties, alternative lexicographic implementations, more symmetry breaking (pp. 16-17).

method_links.note: Symmetry-breaking constraints extended from GNN inputs to general and DAG graph spaces, with completeness proved and strength measured against exact OEIS counts (a labelled oracle, as in step 5)
The generalise-behind-one-interface step applied to the input domain (graph space with shortest paths) that GNN, kernel and molecular models share, rather than to a trained model

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Encoding constraints listed as necessary conditions, then a bijection between the feasible set and the graph space proved by induction on shortest distance

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: distillation paper after an application run
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: States its aim as distilling recent application papers [45-48] into general settings, with proofs and a standalone repository

transferable: Encode derived graph properties as auxiliary variables and specialise to subclasses by adding constraints, not by writing new models (pp. 2-6)
Prove an encoding exact: necessary conditions, linearisation with a named big-M, injectivity by induction on a natural graph quantity (pp. 2-6)
Prove symmetry-breaking completeness with an explicit indexing algorithm whose output satisfies the constraints (pp. 11-15)
Evaluate symmetry breaking by exhaustive solution counting bracketed by the labelled and unlabelled OEIS counts (p. 16)
Label logically redundant constraints as relaxation-tightening (p. 6)

quotes.text: This paper aims to distill the fundamental contributions of our recent works [45, 46, 47, 48] and extend them from specific applications to general settings.

There are often multiple ways to encode a combinatorial problem, but insufficient constraints result in an unnecessarily large search space with symmetric solutions, while excessive constraints may cutoff feasible solutions from the search space.

title: BoGrape: Bayesian optimization over graphs with shortest-path encoded
contribution: A graph Bayesian-optimisation method whose acquisition function is optimised globally as a MIP. It combines a bijective encoding of connected graphs with shortest paths, four shortest-path kernel variants written as linear functions of indicator variables, and problem-specific constraints, and is competitive on random-GNN benchmarks and QM7/QM9 molecular design.
problem_entry: Graph BO either fixes the graph or the graph type, and optimises acquisitions by evolution or sampling, which cannot explore effectively, embed constraints or certify the acquisition optimum that regret theory needs (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Shortest-path kernels (SP, SSP, ESP, ESSP) plus a feature kernel, encoded through the MIP-SP variables and count indicators so that LCB optimisation over graphs and features becomes a MIP, extending PK-MIQP (pp. 3-8).
assumptions: Connected, mainly undirected graphs of fixed or bounded size; one-hot node labels within binary features; PD kernels; noise 1e-6, hyperparameters in [0.01, 100], beta_t^(1/2)=1; global optimality assumed in the theory but the MIP is capped at 600 s in practice (pp. 3-9, 23).
proof_devices: PD of SSP as a special case of SP, and of ESP/ESSP as exponentials of linear-form kernels (Lemmas 3.1-3.2, pp. 4-5)
Bijection between MIP-SP and connected n-node graphs by induction on shortest distance (Thm 3.5, pp. 18-19)
Bounded-size extension by fixing the node count and reducing to MIP-SP (Thm 3.6, p. 19)
Exact linearisation of the quadratic self-kernel by one-hot count indicators (p. 7)
Symmetry of undirected graphs fixes the odd count indicators to zero (p. 20)
experiments: GP prediction on QM7 (RMSE/MNLL tables, 100 replications). BO on random GAT/GCN/GraphSAGE benchmarks (N=10, 20) and QM7/QM9 molecular design (N=10-30) with Limeade constraints: 10 initial points + 50 iterations, 10 replications, mean +/- 0.5 std, 600 s MIP limit. Ablations on time limit, beta_t and baseline candidates (20->100); exclusion of WL-evol quantified (pp. 7-10, 21-30).
positioning: Joins graph BO (Ru et al.'s WL-evol as the state of the art) with MIP over trained models (OMLT, Misic, Mistry, Anderson, Tsay); builds on the group's PK-MIQP and Limeade; says openly that the molecular baselines are not the most advanced (pp. 2-3, 9-10, 23).
writing: Three bulleted contributions, a pipeline figure, an arrow-annotated formulation; Appendix B organised as answers to reviewer questions; leftover '[link to be added after peer review]' and minor index slips (pp. 2-3, 9, 19-23).
limits_future: The computational complexity of the MIP is the main limit; scalability ideas (trust region, time limit, heuristics, fragments); future work: simplify the formulations, relax connectivity (pp. 10, 21).

method_links.note: Step 8 (optimise the acquisition globally as a MIP) carried from tree kernels to graph kernels; step 3 'solve exactly where possible' is the stated motivation
The encoded object is a GP kernel over a combinatorial domain; the trained GNNs are only black-box objectives
Kernel verdict split by graph size (expressive kernels for small graphs, simple kernels for large ones) with no single default; the deciding variable is size, not problem class
Baselines strengthened (Limeade feasibility, 5x candidates) and exclusions quantified by feasibility rates
Self-proposed random-GNN benchmarks with no public link yet, a single machine, 0.5-std bands

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: the encodable model chooses the ML model
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: The authors state that the shortest-path kernel was chosen because their graph-optimisation encoding made it representable, not chosen first
The MIP-SP feasible set is proved to be in bijection with connected graphs by induction on shortest distance

transferable: Write k(x, X_i) as a linear function of indicator variables of x, with coefficients precomputed from each data point (p. 6)
Linearise a quadratic in an integer count exactly with one-hot indicators over its range (p. 7)
Run a time-limit ablation that reports both the BO curve and the average MIP gap (pp. 21-22)
Quantify a baseline's feasibility rate before excluding it; give sampling baselines 5x the candidates (p. 24)
Structure the appendix as titled answers to likely reviewer questions (pp. 20-23)
coauthors: Yilin Xie, Shiqiang Zhang (equal first authors), Jixiang Qing, Calvin Tsay (equal corresponding author with Misener)

quotes.text: Therefore, it is not that we chose shortest-path kernel first for specific reasons then developed necessary formulations, but that the fundamental advances in graph optimization led us to shortest-path kernels.

In other words, finding good feasible solutions is easier (and important for practical BO performance), while closing the MIPgap (important for theoretical BO convergence) requires more computational effort.
